newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright keeps door to NATO-Russia deal open.
newsitem.headline: Albright keeps door to NATO-Russia deal open.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright left Russia on Friday with no breakthrough in the row over NATO's eastward expansion plans, but she at least succeeded in keeping open the door to agreement.
Some Russians had predicted hostility at the talks in Moscow and ruled out any chance of doing business with a woman who fled communist rule in her native Czechoslovakia half a century ago.
But Albright, who spoke Russian with President Boris Yeltsin, and her hosts were determined not to let talks collapse before next month's Russian-U.S. summit in Helsinki.
By making proposals on how the alliance and Russia could build real cooperation, she hoped to leave the impression that NATO is seriously trying to address Moscow's worries.

"She brought proposals which may not be significant on their own or change the nature of relations, but the West has shown it is trying to accommodate Russia's concerns," said Andrei Kortunov, head of the Russian Science Foundation think-tank.

"Both sides were concerned by the prospect of failure and there was a lot of speculation here that it would fail completely. But both sides have shown they want to keep the door open to further negotiations."

During her visit, officials from President Boris Yeltsin down maintained their fierce opposition to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to admit Moscow's former Cold War allies in eastern Europe.

The risk of a major clash over NATO was high. Russian leaders have stepped up their verbal campaign against expansion in recent weeks, saying it will open divisions in Europe, threaten Russia's security and undermine Yeltsin.

But the pleasantries from officials on both sides and the lack of strong words at a joint news conference with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov pointed to a mutual interest in keeping relations on track.
Albright's spokesman, Nicholas Burns, even quoted Primakov as saying: "I'm going to be nice to you."

Moscow was probably never intended to be a forum for major breakthroughs over NATO enlargement. Hopes have been pinned instead on Yeltsin's planned summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki on March 20 and 21.

Officials from both countries regarded Albright's trip primarily as a chance to establish a working relationship following her appointment last month and an opportunity to map out areas where progress might be made in Helsinki.

For Moscow, it was an opportunity to test NATO's willingness to make concessions. For Washington, it was a chance to gauge Yeltsin's ability to rule after pneumonia and heart problems -- Albright said he seemed "very much in charge".
The Secretary of State signalled no major change in U.S. policy. She remained opposed to Russia's main demand for joint decision-making with NATO on matters which touch its security interests.
But she and NATO presented proposals during her tour of Europe this week which at least went some way to taking account of Russia's concerns over NATO enlargement.

They included reducing conventional weapons in Europe under proposed modifications to a 1990 treaty limiting the numbers of such arms and where they can be placed. This addressed Russian fears of a NATO build-up on its borders.

Albright also suggested creating a joint NATO-Russian brigade, mainly for peacekeeping purposes, to show goodwill. The Kremlin said on Friday it was unimpressed by the proposal, criticised by nationalist and communist opponents.
"Many people feel disappointed by the results of her visit and say she brought nothing significant," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy director of the USA and Canada Institute think-tank.
"But in the sea of disappointment, I see signs of a possible agreement. The trial balloons have been raised and there are slightly better grounds to hope for an agreement by July."
Kremenyuk was referring to the month in which NATO holds a summit in Madrid to offer membership invitations, probably to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Both NATO and Russia want an agreement by then to chart out their relationship, fearing failure to do so would send the temperature between East and West plummeting.

The hint of progress, and the hope that Moscow believes NATO is now hearing its voice, is vital for Yeltsin to reassure the Russian people over enlargement. Without confidence that he can do so, an agreement may prove impossible.
"It is important for Yeltsin to have something to sell the Russian people and political establishment," said Alexei Pushkov, a commentator for the Moscow News newspaper.
"These negotiations do not change the character of the U.S. position or take in the Russian proposals in their entirety, but there is a slight change for the better in the atmosphere."
